# Head and neck region

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Ear, nose, and throat > Basics of ENT > Head and neck region*

[Original Article Link](/library/b60HjS)

---

## Summary

This chapter gives an overview of the important structures, muscles, <u>fasciae</u>, and vessels (<u>arteries</u>, <u>veins</u>, <u>lymph</u>, nerves) of the head and neck region. The <u>brain</u>, one of the most important organs, is protected by the <u>skull</u>, both of which are covered in other articles. There are also individual articles for the organs of perception as well as for the <u>thyroid gland</u>, the <u>salivary glands</u>, <u>teeth</u> and <u>oral cavity</u>. The head and neck region is the beginning of the respiratory and digestive tract, both of which also have their own articles.

---

## Regions

### Regions of the head




The head is divided into 14 regions:



1. * Frontal region
2. * Parietal region
3. * Occipital region
4. * Temporal region
5. * Auricular region
6. * Mastoid region
7. * Facial region
1. * Orbital region
2. * Infraorbital region
3. * Nasal region
4. * Zygomatic region
5. * Buccal region
6. * <u>Parotid</u> region
7. * Oral region
8. * Mental region




![Regions of the head and neck](media/iw0cisgni8pxuudup7bfup1t.jpg)

Regions of the head and neck




### Regions of the neck




* The <u>sternocleidomastoid muscle</u>, <u>trapezius</u>, and <u>clavicle</u> are important landmarks for orientation on the neck.

* At the <u>anterior</u> midline, the <u>laryngeal prominence</u> forms the “Adam's Apple” due to the underlying <u>thyroid</u> <u>cartilage</u>.

* The <u>hyoid bone</u> can be palpated between the <u>laryngeal prominence</u> and the chin.

* The neck is divided into 4 regions
1. * <u>Sternocleidomastoid</u> region
2. * <u>Posterior</u> cervical region
3. * <u>Lateral cervical region</u>
4. * <u>Anterior</u> cervical region





#### Anterior cervical triangle




* Borders

* <u>Anterior</u>: midline in front of the neck

* Superior: <u>mandible</u>

* Inferolateral: <u>sternocleidomastoid muscle</u>

* Triangles: subdivided into four smaller triangles by the <u>digastric</u> and omohyoid muscles

* Submandibular triangle

* Bounded by <u>mandible</u> and the two bellies of the <u>digastric muscle</u>

* Contains submandibular <u>salivary glands</u>, <u>hypoglossal nerve</u>, and facial <u>artery</u>

* Carotid triangle 

* Bounded by the <u>sternocleidomastoid muscle</u>, <u>posterior</u> belly of <u>digastric muscle</u>, and superior belly of omohyoid muscle

* Contains carotid <u>artery</u>, <u>internal jugular vein</u>, and <u>vagus nerve</u>

* Muscular triangle

* Bounded by the midline, <u>hyoid bone</u>, <u>sternocleidomastoid muscle</u>, and superior belly of the omohyoid muscle

* Contains <u>thyroid</u> and <u>parathyroid glands</u>

* Submental triangle: bounded by <u>mandible</u>, hyoid, and <u>anterior</u> belly of <u>digastric muscle</u>





![Carotid triangle](media/gm59wkvex6dmmbr4gxxh5lgk.jpg)

Carotid triangle

![Sternocleidomastoid muscle and lesser supraclavicular fossa](media/xsa5zdncibxhmx50v83dg4ak.jpg)

![Lower half of the face (side view)](media/h7tjj83ggv41jewn4qmhygzq.jpg)

#### Posterior cervical triangle




* Borders

* <u>Posterior</u>: <u>trapezius muscle</u>

* Inferior: <u>clavicle</u>

* Anterosuperior: <u>sternocleidomastoid muscle</u>

* Triangles: subdivided into two smaller triangles by the omohyoid muscle

* Occipital triangle

* Bounded by the <u>sternocleidomastoid</u>, <u>trapezius</u>, and omohyoid muscles

* Contains the <u>brachial plexus</u>, omohyoid muscles, and <u>accessory nerve</u>

* Subclavian triangle

* Bounded by inferior belly of omohyoid muscle, <u>clavicle</u>, and the <u>sternocleidomastoid muscle</u>

* Contains the subclavian muscles, <u>brachial plexus</u>, and <u>external jugular vein</u>










### Suboccipital triangle




* Position: paired region in the deep area of the neck that is covered by the <u>trapezius muscle</u>, splenius muscle, and <u>semispinalis</u> capitis

* Borders

* <u>Cranial</u>: <u>rectus capitis posterior major</u>

* <u>Caudal</u>: <u>obliquus capitis inferior</u>

* <u>Lateral</u>: <u>obliquus capitis superior</u>

* Anatomical structures within

* <u>Vertebral artery</u>

* <u>Vertebral venous plexus</u>

* Suboccipital nerve

## Musculature

### Head muscles




#### Muscles of facial expression




* Move the <u>skin</u> of the face, the alar wings of the nose, the eyelids, and <u>lips</u>

* Enable us to express emotions

* Not connected to bones but only to the <u>skin</u>

* Do not have <u>fasciae</u>

* All innervated by the <u>facial nerve</u>





##### Muscles of the <u>cranium</u>




| Muscle | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Occipitofrontalis muscle | <br>* Movement of the forehead and the brow<br><br> |
| Temporoparietal muscle | <br>* Pulls the <u>ears</u> <u>cranial</u> and <u>dorsal</u><br><br> |





##### Muscles of <u>the ear</u>




| Muscle | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Anterior auricular muscle | <br>* Pulls <u>the ear</u> to the front<br><br> |
| Superior auricular muscle | <br>* Pulls <u>the ear</u> cranially<br><br> |
| Posterior auricular muscle | <br>* Pulls <u>the ear</u> backward<br><br> |





##### <u>Muscles of the eye</u>




| Muscle | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Orbicularis oculi | <br><br>* <u>Eyelid</u> closure<br><br>* Squeezing the eyes shut<br><br>* Blinking<br><br>* Animation of the <u>lacrimal sac</u><br><br><br> |
| Corrugator supercilii | <br>* Draw eyebrows together creating vertical fold (frown line)<br><br> |





##### Muscles of the nose




| Muscle | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Nasalis | <br><br>* Has two parts with opposing functions: tightening and widening of the nostrils<br><br>* Draws the tip of the nose <u>caudal</u><br><br><br> |
| Depressor septi nasi | <br>* Pulls the nose inferiorly; opening the nostrils<br><br> |
| Procerus | <br>* Pulls the <u>skin</u> between the eyebrows <u>caudal</u><br><br> |





##### Muscles of the mouth




| Muscle |  | Function |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Orbicularis oris |  | <br><br>* Closes the mouth<br><br>* Purses the <u>lips</u><br><br><br> |
| Buccinator |  | <br>* Pulls cheeks inwards against the <u>teeth</u> while chewing<br><br> |
| Upper group | Levator labii superioris, levator labii superioris alaeque nasi muscle, risorius, levator anguli oris, zygomaticus major, zygomaticus minor | <br>* Lift upper lip and draw the corners of the mouth upwards (smiling)<br><br> |
| Lower group | Depressor anguli oris, depressor labii inferioris, mentalis | <br><br>* Draw down the lower lip and the corners of the mouth<br><br>* <u>Mentalis</u>: raises lower lip and chin of the <u>skin</u> (pouting muscle)<br><br><br> |





For <u>mastication</u> muscles and muscles of the <u>tongue</u>, see “<u>Oral cavity</u>.”




> [!NOTE]
> The <u>facial nerve</u> (VII) innervates all <u>muscles of facial expression</u>.




#### Hyoid bone and hyoid muscles




* The <u>hyoid bone</u> is a small U-shaped bone with two lesser horns (<u>lateral</u>) and two greater horns (<u>posterior</u>).

* It is positioned cranially to the <u>thyroid</u> <u>cartilage</u> and is connected to it via the thyrohyoid membrane.

* The hyoid muscles are distinguished into <u>suprahyoid muscles</u> (<u>cranial</u> to the <u>hyoid bone</u>) and <u>infrahyoid muscles</u> (<u>caudal</u> to the <u>hyoid bone</u>).





| Muscle |  |  |  | Function | Innervation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <br>Suprahyoid muscles (Digastric, stylohyoid, mylohyoid, geniohyoid) |  |  |  | <br><br>* Form the bottom of the mouth<br><br>* Elevate the <u>hyoid bone</u> during <u>swallowing</u><br><br>* Support the opening of the <u>jaw</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Inferior alveolar nerve (mylohyoid and <u>anterior</u> belly of <u>digastric</u>)<br><br>* <u>Facial nerve</u> (<u>stylohyoid</u> and <u>posterior</u> belly of <u>digastric</u>)<br><br>* <u>Anterior</u> ramus of the <u>spinal nerve</u> C1 (via the <u>hypoglossal nerve</u>)<br><br><br> |
| <br>Infrahyoid muscles (Sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid, omohyoid) |  |  |  | <br>* Depress the <u>larynx</u> and <u>hyoid bone</u> after <u>swallowing</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Ansa cervicalis</u> from the <u>cervical plexus</u> (C1–C3), except the thyrohyoid muscle that is innervated by a branch of the <u>anterior rami</u> of the C1 <u>spinal nerve</u><br><br> |

### Neck muscles




The musculature of the neck can be differentiated into <u>superficial</u> and deep muscles.




#### <u>Superficial</u> muscles of the neck




| Muscle | Characteristics | Function | Innervation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sternocleidomastoid | <br><br>* Prominent muscle on the sides of the neck<br><br>* Arises from <u>sternum</u> and <u>clavicle</u> and inserts into the <u>mastoid process</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Unilateral contraction<br><br>* Flexes the head laterally on the <u>ipsilateral</u> side<br><br>* Rotates the head to the <u>contralateral</u> side<br><br>* Bilateral contraction: flexes neck dorsally<br><br>* Accessory respiratory muscle<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Motor: <u>accessory nerve</u> (XI)<br><br>* Sensation: <u>cervical plexus</u> (C2–C3)<br><br><br> |
| Platysma | <br>* Broad <u>superficial</u> muscle that runs subcutaneously from the upper chest area to the lower jawbone (<u>mandible</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* Reinforces the <u>skin</u> of the neck<br><br>* Pulls <u>lips</u> to the sides and down<br><br>* Opens <u>jaw</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Cervical branch of the <u>facial nerve</u><br><br> |





![Sternocleidomastoid muscle](media/rcwn65wew4ngr166znzdji4i.jpg)

Sternocleidomastoid muscle

![Sternocleidomastoid muscle and lesser supraclavicular fossa](media/xsa5zdncibxhmx50v83dg4ak.jpg)

Sternocleidomastoid muscle and lesser supraclavicular fossa




> [!NOTE]
> An abnormal tone or length of the <u>sternocleidomastoid muscle</u> has a variety of mechanisms (e.g., trauma, muscle tone disorders, congenital muscle tightness, extrinsic masses, ocular, etc.) and is referred to as <u>torticollis</u> (<u>wry neck</u>).




#### Deep muscles of the neck




* Move the <u>cervical spine</u>

* Partly act as accessory muscles for respiration

* Branches of the <u>cervical plexus</u> and <u>brachial plexus</u> innervate the deep neck muscles.





| Group |  | Origin | Insertion | <br>Function<br> | Innervation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Scalene muscles | Anterior scalene | <br>* <u>Transverse processes</u> of <u>cervical vertebrae</u> (C2–C7)<br><br> | <br>* First or second <u>rib</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Accessory respiratory muscles: lift the upper <u>ribs</u><br><br>* Unilateral: <u>ipsilateral</u> <u>flexion</u> of the head<br><br>* Bilateral: <u>flexion</u> of the neck<br><br><br> | <br>* Branches of the <u>cervical plexus</u> and <u>brachial plexus</u> (C3–C8)<br><br> |
| Middle scalene |  |  |  |  |  |
| Posterior scalene |  |  |  |  |  |
| Prevertebral muscles | Longus colli muscle | <br>* <u>Transverse processes</u> of C5–T3<br><br> | <br>* <u>Atlas</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Unilateral: <u>ipsilateral</u> <u>flexion</u> of the head<br><br>* Bilateral: stabilization and rotation of the head<br><br><br> | <br>* Branches of the <u>cervical plexus</u> (C1–C6)<br><br> |
| Longus capitis muscle | <br>* <u>Transverse processes</u> of C3–C6<br><br> | <br>* <u>Occipital bone</u><br><br> |  |  |  |
| <br>Rectus capitis anterior<br> | <br>* <u>Atlas</u><br><br> |  |  |  |  |
| Rectus capitis lateralis | <br>* <u>Transverse process</u> of the <u>atlas</u><br><br> |  |  |  |  |
| Suboccipital muscles | Obliquus capitis superior | <br>* <u>Transverse process</u> of the <u>atlas</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Lateral</u> part of the inferior nuchal line<br><br> | <br><br>* Unilateral: <u>ipsilateral</u> <u>flexion</u> and rotation of the head<br><br>* Bilateral: <u>dorsal</u> extension of the head<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Posterior</u> branch of suboccipital nerve (C1)<br><br> |
| Rectus capitis posterior minor | <br>* <u>Posterior</u> tubercle of the <u>atlas</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Medial</u> part of the inferior nuchal line<br><br> |  |  |  |
| Rectus capitis posterior major | <br>* <u>Spinous process</u> of the axis<br><br> |  |  |  |  |
| Obliquus capitis inferior | <br>* <u>Transverse process</u> of the <u>atlas</u><br><br> |  |  |  |  |

## Fascias

### Fascias of the head




* Temporal <u>fascia</u>: covers temporal muscle

* <u>Parotid</u> <u>fascia</u>: covers the <u>parotid gland</u>

* Masseteric <u>fascia</u>: covers <u>muscles of mastication</u>

* Buccopharyngeal fascia: a layer of <u>fascia</u> that spans between the <u>carotid sheaths</u>, <u>posterior</u> to the <u>esophagus</u> and the <u>lateral</u> lobes of the <u>thyroid gland</u>





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Muscles of facial expression</u> do not have a <u>fascia</u> as they are placed directly under the <u>skin</u>.




### Fascias of the neck




Because the structures in the neck region are very close to each other, there are many <u>fasciae</u> that ensheath and separate (compartmentalize) the different structures.




#### Superficial cervical fascia




* Position: lies between the <u>skin</u> and the <u>deep cervical fascia</u>

* Surrounds:

* <u>Subcutaneous fat</u> tissue

* <u>Platysma muscle</u>

* <u>Superficial</u> nerves, <u>veins</u>, and <u>lymph nodes</u>





#### Deep cervical fascia




* Investing layer

* Surrounds:

* <u>Sternocleidomastoid muscle</u>

* <u>Trapezius muscle</u>

* Position: directly under the <u>platysma muscle</u>

* Carotid sheath

* Surrounds:

* <u>Common carotid artery</u>

* <u>Internal carotid artery</u>

* <u>Internal jugular vein</u>

* <u>Vagus nerve</u>

* Keeps the <u>internal jugular vein</u> open due to negative pressure

* Pretracheal layer
* Surrounds:

* <u>Esophagus</u>

* <u>Trachea</u>

* <u>Thyroid gland</u>

* <u>Infrahyoid muscles</u>

* Prevertebral layer

* Surrounds:

* Muscles

* Deep muscles of the neck

* <u>Levator scapulae muscle</u>

* Intrinsic muscles of the neck

* Vasculature and nerves

* <u>Sympathetic trunk</u>

* <u>Brachial plexus</u>

* <u>Subclavian artery</u>

* <u>Phrenic nerve</u>

* Attachment

* Cranially: <u>occipital bone</u>

* <u>Caudally</u>: merges with the endothoracic <u>fascia</u> and the <u>anterior longitudinal ligament</u>





> [!NOTE]
> The <u>prevertebral layer</u> of the <u>deep cervical fascia</u> extends from the <u>skull</u> via the <u>mediastinum</u> to the <u>diaphragm</u>. Therefore, infections in this layer can cause great harm.

## Vasculature, lymphatic drainage, and innervation

### <u>Arteries</u>




* The <u>common carotid arteries</u> and <u>subclavian arteries</u> supply the head and neck.

* The <u>common carotid artery</u> splits into the <u>internal carotid artery</u>, supplying mainly intracranial regions, and the <u>external carotid artery</u>, supplying mainly extracranial regions.

* The <u>subclavian artery</u> supplies the lower regions of the neck, close to the thorax.





#### Subclavian artery




![Subclavian artery and its branches](media/nlzw72e6q9vzjev7kl9ncwi5.jpg)

Subclavian artery and its branches

![Arteries of the upper extremity](media/pczabpv1mfqwjuigejhxhtfp.jpg)

Arteries of the upper extremity




* Origin

* Left subclavian artery: direct branch of the aorta

* Right subclavian artery: a branch from the brachiocephalic <u>artery</u>

* Branches 

* Internal thoracic artery

* <u>Vertebral artery</u>

* Thyrocervical trunk

* Costocervical trunk





> [!NOTE]
> In stenosis of the <u>coronary arteries</u>, the <u>internal thoracic artery</u> can be used as a natural <u>coronary artery bypass graft</u>.




> [!NOTE]
> A stenosis of the <u>subclavian artery</u> <u>proximal</u> to the origin of the <u>vertebral artery</u> may result in <u>subclavian steal syndrome</u>.




![Branches of the vertebral artery and the costocervical trunk](media/jq7g9uofkys8fxuc4266hza7.jpg)

Branches of the vertebral artery and the costocervical trunk




#### Common carotid arteries




![Arterial supply of the face and neck](media/p7d2fuuoqhtxdb47c7xlxj7e.jpg)

Arterial supply of the face and neck




* Origin

* Left side: direct branch of the aorta

* Right side: a branch from the brachiocephalic <u>artery</u>

* Course: ascend in the neck within the <u>carotid sheath</u>

* Branches on each side: form the carotid bifurcation at the level of C4 

* <u>Internal carotid artery</u>

* <u>External carotid artery</u>





> [!NOTE]
> The <u>common carotid arteries</u> bifourcate at the level of C4.




> [!NOTE]
> An increased <u>carotid sinus</u> <u>sensitivity</u> can result in <u>syncopes</u> due to low systolic blood pressure when pressure is applied to the <u>carotid sinus</u>. It is frequently associated with arteriosclerotic changes in the <u>carotid sinus</u>.




##### Internal carotid artery




* Origin: arises from the <u>common carotid</u> at the level of the upper border of the <u>thyroid</u> <u>cartilage</u>

* Course: enters the <u>skull</u> via the <u>carotid canal</u> of the <u>temporal bone</u>

* Branches 

* <u>Ophthalmic artery</u>

* <u>Anterior cerebral artery</u>

* <u>Middle cerebral artery</u>

* <u>Circle of Willis</u>

* No branches in the neck





![Left internal carotid artery (medial view)](media/rf94vcqv10lchwvvxf3n3odi.jpg)

Left internal carotid artery (medial view)




##### External carotid artery




* Origin: arises from the <u>common carotid</u> at the level of the upper border of the <u>thyroid</u> <u>cartilage</u>

* Branches  

* Superior <u>thyroid</u> <u>artery</u>

* <u>Lingual artery</u>

* Facial <u>artery</u>

* Ascending pharyngeal artery

* Occipital <u>artery</u>

* <u>Posterior</u> auricular <u>artery</u>

* Maxillary <u>arteries</u>

* Superficial temporal artery





> [!NOTE]
> The <u>temporal artery</u> is involved in <u>giant cell arteritis</u>.




> [!NOTE]
> A branch of the maxillary <u>artery</u> is the middle meningeal artery. It enters the <u>skull</u> through the <u>foramen spinosum</u> and mostly supplies the <u>meninges</u> and the <u>skull</u>. A craniocerebral injury can result in rupture or <u>laceration</u> of the <u>middle meningeal artery</u>, leading to the life-threatening condition of an <u>epidural hematoma</u>.

### <u>Veins</u>




#### <u>Superficial veins</u>




##### External jugular vein




* Collects blood from the exterior <u>cranium</u> and parts of the face

* Begins at the <u>parotid gland</u> and extends downwards

* Runs along the side of the neck

* Covered by the <u>platysma</u>

* Pierces through the <u>superficial</u> layer of the <u>fascia</u> of the neck

* Ends in the <u>venous angle</u> or in the <u>internal jugular vein</u>





#### <u>Deep veins</u>




##### Internal jugular vein




* Collects blood from the <u>brain</u>, parts of the face, and neck

* Continuation of the sigmoid sinus at the <u>jugular foramen</u>

* Begins at the <u>base of the skull</u> and extends downwards

* Ends in the <u>brachiocephalic vein</u> → <u>superior vena cava</u>





##### Subclavian vein




* Drains venous blood from the arms

* Runs along the front of the <u>anterior scalene muscle</u> (anteriomedial to the <u>scalene triangle</u>)

* Ends in the <u>venous angle</u>, where it forms the <u>brachiocephalic vein</u> with the <u>internal jugular vein</u>





![Jugular veins](media/yakt1etrgsicsa8xn55ua8a8.jpg)

Jugular veins

### <u>Lymphatics</u>




* About one-third of the <u>lymph nodes</u> of the body are located in the head and neck area as the beginning of the respiratory and digestive tract is <u>prone</u> to many pathogens.

* All <u>lymphatic drainage</u> ends in the left and right jugular <u>lymph</u> trunk.

* On the right side, this trunk ends in the junction of the internal jugular and <u>subclavian veins</u>, called the venous angle.

* On the left side, it joins the <u>thoracic duct</u>.

* For details, see “<u>Lymph nodes of the head and neck</u>.”

| Superficial cervical lymph nodes |  | <br><br>* Accompany the<br><br>* <u>External jugular vein</u> (<u>posterior cervical triangle</u>)<br><br>* <u>Anterior</u> jugular <u>vein</u> (<u>anterior cervical triangle</u>)<br><br>* Drain into the <u>deep cervical lymph nodes</u><br><br><br> |
| Deep cervical lymph nodes | Superior | <br><br>* Accompany the <u>internal jugular vein</u> (<u>carotid triangle</u>)<br><br>* Form the jugular trunk that ends on the<br><br>* Right side: into the <u>venous angle</u> (junction of <u>internal jugular vein</u> and <u>subclavian vein</u>)<br><br>* Left side: into the <u>thoracic duct</u><br><br><br> |
| Inferior | <br>* Located on the <u>internal jugular vein</u> close to the <u>subclavian vein</u><br><br> |  |

### Nerves




* Nerves of the head and neck region include:

* <u>Cranial nerves</u> (see <u>cranial nerve disorders</u>)

* <u>Parasympathetic</u> cervical <u>ganglia</u>

* <u>Sympathetic</u> cervical <u>ganglia</u> (see <u>autonomic nervous system</u> for more details)

* Branches of the <u>spinal nerves</u>

* The <u>ventral</u> branches of the <u>spinal nerves</u> (C1–C4) form the <u>cervical plexus</u> and have sensory and motor branches.





#### Cervical plexus




![Cervical plexus](media/onwaa5etvxpiezmsktnnl6d2.jpg)

Cervical plexus




Description: A nerve plexus composed of the <u>anterior rami</u> of the cervical <u>nerve roots</u>, which provides motor and sensory innervation to most neck muscles and the area over the <u>anterior</u> and <u>lateral</u> neck.




| Nerve | Spinal segment | Innervation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ansa cervicalis | C1–C3 | <br>* Motor<br>* <u>Infrahyoid muscles</u> (omohyoid, sternohyoid, and sternothyroid muscles)<br><br> |
| Phrenic nerve | C3–C5 | <br><br>* Motor: <u>diaphragm</u><br><br>* Sensory <br><br>* <u>Pleura</u> (<u>mediastinal</u>)<br><br>* <u>Pericardium</u><br><br><br> |
| Lesser occipital nerve | C2, C3 | <br>* Sensory<br><br>* Scalp<br><br>* <u>Ear</u><br><br>* Neck<br><br>* Upper thorax<br><br> |
| Great auricular nerve | C2, C3 |  |
| Transverse cervical nerve | C2, C3 |  |
| Supraclavicular nerve | C3, C4 |  |
| <br><u>Posterior</u> branches of cervical nerves Suboccipital nerve, Greater occipital nerve, Third occipital nerve | C1–C3 | <br><br>* Sensory: occiput and neck<br><br>* Motor (suboccipital nerve): <u>suboccipital muscles</u><br><br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Phrenic nerve</u>: C3, C4, C5 – keep the <u>diaphragm</u> alive!




> [!NOTE]
> A <u>mediastinal</u> <u>tumor</u> can present with <u>shortness of breath</u>, shoulder <u>pain</u>, and <u>hiccups</u> due to irritation of the <u>phrenic nerve</u>.

## Embryology

Many structures in the head and neck have their origin in the <u>pharyngeal arches</u>, <u>pharyngeal pouches</u>, and <u>pharyngeal grooves</u>. For a detailed description of these see <u>branchial apparatus</u>.

---

## Clinical significance

### Head




* Diseases of <u>salivary gland</u>

* <u>Sinusitis</u>

* <u>Otitis externa</u>

* <u>Acute otitis media</u>

* <u>Chronic otitis media</u>

* <u>Hearing loss</u>

* Diseases of <u>retina</u>

* <u>Facial nerve palsy</u>





### Neck




* Diseases of <u>salivary gland</u>

* <u>Goiter</u>

* <u>Thyroid nodules</u>

* <u>Thyroid cancer</u>

* <u>Thoracic outlet syndrome</u>

* <u>Laryngitis</u>

* <u>Acute tonsillitis</u>

* <u>Pharyngitis</u>, see: <u>differential diagnosis of tonsillitis</u>

* Clinical assessment of <u>central venous pressure</u>
